title: Current, resistance and circuits
note: Current is the rate charge flows, and resistance sets how much current a voltage drives: V = IR. Series elements share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage. Kirchhoff's rules are conservation of charge at junctions and conservation of energy around loops.

read.title: How circuits share
text: A battery maintains a potential difference between its terminals, and when a conducting path connects them, charge flows. The flow rate is the current, measured in amperes, coulombs per second. Each electron actually drifts very slowly, well under a millimeter per second, but the electric field that pushes them spreads through the wire almost instantly, so a lamp lights the moment you flip the switch.

Resistance measures how much a component opposes current. For many materials the current is proportional to the voltage, V = IR, which is Ohm's law. Resistance grows with a wire's length and shrinks with its cross-sectional area.

When resistors are in series, the same current passes through each, and their resistances add. In parallel, each branch sees the same voltage, and adding branches gives charge more paths, so the total resistance drops below that of the smallest branch. Homes are wired in parallel: every appliance gets the full outlet voltage, and each one you switch on draws more total current from the circuit. A breaker trips when that total climbs too high.
Kirchhoff's two rules handle any circuit: current into a junction equals current out, and potential changes around a closed loop sum to zero.
